name: Yusuf Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the month. I work for the Lacey estate, about six hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape. This time of year, November, it's drilling the last of the winter wheat and servicing kit in the workshop. Harvest, it's fourteen-hour days on the combine. I like being out on my own in the tractor with the radio on, honestly. What wears me out is the paperwork side, spray records and that, which the farm manager keeps saying I should do on the tablet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. The tractor's got GPS steering, which I'll admit is handy on a long field, but that's the boss's choice, not mine. I don't use the chat things. I don't see the point. I live with Leah, she teaches at the primary school, in a rented place on Station Road. We've got about two months' worth saved, three if you count the money for the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the same as now, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go. I'm not one for big predictions. Things change slower than people say, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be glad. I don't want to learn a whole new system. If the computer does the spray records, great, as long as I don't have to talk to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Drill the wheat, run the combine, service the kit. Maybe I'd let the manager show me the tablet records, because he'll keep asking. And we'd keep saving for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're saving for a deposit. How long would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At this rate, five or six years, if nothing goes wrong. Leah's on a teacher's wage and I'm on a farm wage. It's not fast but it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work you'd like a machine to take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greasing the combine. Two hours of lying under it every morning in harvest. If AI fixed that I'd shake its hand. But that's not really AI, is it, that's just better engineering.

S0.say: I'd say things change slower than people claim, they always do. I'm not one for big predictions and this would just show it.
S0.think: Privately he'd be glad not to learn a new system. If the computer does the spray records he's happy, as long as he doesn't have to talk to it.
S0.do: Carries on drilling, harvesting and servicing machinery as usual. Lets the manager show him the tablet records and keeps saving slowly with his partner for a house deposit.
S0.quote: If the computer does the spray records, great, as long as I don't have to talk to it.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is calm, plain-spoken and wary of predictions. He tolerates technology chosen by his boss but won't seek it out. His long-term goal is a modest one: a house deposit in five or six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds likely enough, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how farming's always gone. My granddad had five men on this estate, now there's me and two others. It's sad but it's the way of it. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. Grain's the easiest farming to automate. Flat fields, same job up and down. If the estate gets a self-driving tractor, one of the three of us goes, and I'm not the most senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit, see what the estate actually buys. I'd stop thinking about a new truck and put that money in savings. If it came to it I'd ask about the workshop side, because someone has to fix the self-driving kit when it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. That feeling when the combine makes a noise you don't recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate next door laid off their tractor driver. That'd be a sign. Until then, I'm not going to panic about something on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the most senior of the three of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete. He's been there thirty years. And Arjun's the manager's nephew, so you can guess. That leaves me. I hadn't really said that out loud before.

S1.say: I'd say it's how farming's always gone, with fewer workers each generation. It's sad but that's the way of it, and I wouldn't make a fuss.
S1.think: Privately he worries because flat grain fields are the easiest farming to automate. If the estate buys a self-driving tractor, one of three workers goes and he's not the most senior.
S1.do: Waits to see what the estate buys and puts truck money into savings instead. If needed, asks to move to workshop work fixing the self-driving machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise from the combine he doesn't recognise.
S1.quote: My granddad had five men on this estate, now there's me and two others.
S1.fieldNote: Publicly he shrugs; privately he's done the maths and knows he'd be the one let go. He doesn't blame anyone, seeing it as how farming has always gone. He'd only act once he saw a layoff nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Next harvest and one more. Then that's it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should've slowed it down. I'm not political, but that's too fast for anybody. I'd say that to anyone, even the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm gone by the second harvest. A machine that can drive, fix itself and fill in the records doesn't need me. And I don't know what else I'd do. I've only ever done this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, straight away. No holiday, cancel the gym, sell the old motorbike. Then, I don't know. I'd look for anything going: driving, warehouse, labouring. And I'd probably lean on Leah's wage for a bit, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A heavy feeling in my stomach. Like the bank's called you in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Driving and warehouse work could go too in this picture. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That's the bit that gets me. I'd be looking for the same kind of job everyone else is looking for, and those go too. I honestly don't know. I'd have to ask someone cleverer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years change, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's too short to learn anything. I'm slow at new things, I know that. Give me five years and maybe I'd do a course. Two years, I'd just be grabbing whatever's nearest.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and someone should have slowed it down. He isn't political, but he'd tell anyone, even the boss, that it's too fast.
S2.think: Privately he expects to be gone by the second harvest, because a machine that drives, fixes itself and does the records doesn't need him. He's never done any other work.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard at once, cancelling the holiday and gym and selling his old motorbike. Looks for any driving, warehouse or labouring work and leans on his partner's teaching wage for a while.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a heavy feeling like being called in by the bank.
S2.quote: I'd be looking for the same kind of job everyone else is looking for, and those go too.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks his usual calm. He knows the jobs he'd run to are exposed too, and admits he has no answer. Relying on his partner's wage clearly hurts his pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick. But you'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: too fast. But I'd also say people should get ready, not just moan. That's a bit rich coming from me, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably wait a year or two longer than I should. That's me. But I'd know the self-driving kit is coming and someone has to keep it running in a muddy field at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep working, save every spare bit, aim for six months. Year two, if I saw the machines arriving, I'd do the agricultural engineering course at the college, evenings. Leah would make me. I'd still avoid the chat things until someone made me use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd be doing something, so not as bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait longer than you should. What would get you moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah, honestly. She plans everything. She'd print the course form and leave it on the kitchen table. That's how I ended up doing the forklift licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would fixing self-driving tractors mean using AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I'd have to. I'd do it if it paid. I wouldn't like it, but I'd do it, same as the GPS. You get used to things.

S3.say: I'd say it's still too fast, but people should get ready instead of moaning. He admits that's a bit rich coming from him.
S3.think: Privately he expects to wait a year or two longer than he should. He knows someone will have to keep self-driving kit running in muddy fields.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves toward six months in the first year. In year two, starts an evening agricultural engineering course at the local college, pushed along by his partner.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less so because he'd be doing something.
S3.quote: She'd print the course form and leave it on the kitchen table.
S3.fieldNote: He's very honest about his own slowness and who gets him moving. Five years is enough for a practical plan: fix the machines that replace him. He'd accept AI tools only if the pay made it worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, that's a long way off, and they've said this stuff before. I wouldn't say much, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the dangerous one for me. I'd put it off. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, and then it'd be year eight and I'd still be on the combine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm being sensible, which I'd try to be: keep the job, buy a house with Leah in about five years while I'm still earning, and do the engineering course around year three. Keep saving. That's the plan Leah would write, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the surface. Uneasy underneath, because I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house in this picture, when your job's at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Leah's job is safer than mine, I reckon, and we'd want something solid before the change. If I'm going to retrain, I'd rather do it with a roof that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm scared but I'd move because I'd have to. Ten years, I'm not scared enough to move. Funny that. The slow one might catch me out more.

S4.say: I'd say it's a long way off and they've said this stuff before. He wouldn't say much about it in public.
S4.think: Privately he sees ten years as dangerous for him, because he'd put it off until year eight. He knows his habit of waiting.
S4.do: Keeps the job and aims to buy a house with his partner in about five years. Plans to start the engineering course around year three and keeps saving steadily.
S4.feel: Calm on the surface and uneasy underneath, because he knows himself.
S4.quote: Ten years, I'm not scared enough to move.
S4.fieldNote: Yusuf sees the longest warning as the one most likely to catch him out. His plans lean on his partner's organising and her more secure job. He is the most self-aware about delay of any farmer in this group so far.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, two harvests, and I've only ever driven a tractor. What would help is a proper course, paid, with the college, for people like me who are good with machines but not with screens. And somebody telling us early, not on the news.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the estate. Old Mr Lacey's family have farmed it two hundred years. I don't know what they'd do. Maybe they'd be fine. But I'd like to know if they'd look after the three of us.

headlineQuote: Ten years, I'm not scared enough to move.
portrait: Yusuf Young is a 27-year-old tractor and combine driver on a 600-hectare grain estate, who likes his days alone in the cab and has never used an AI tool. He lives with his partner Leah, a primary teacher, and they have about two months saved toward a house. He's pragmatic, doesn't blame anyone and sees fewer farm jobs as the way things have always gone. He knows grain is easy to automate and that he'd be the first of three workers to go. In the fast picture he grabs at any job; with more warning he plans an engineering course, though he admits ten years might make him wait too long.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two harvests isn't enough time to learn anything other than driving a tractor.
whatWouldHelp: A paid college course for people good with machines but not screens, and early warning from employers rather than from the news.
